en.title: Agriculture: the whole course
en.short: What agriculture is, how an agriculture degree is organised, the main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What agriculture is
sections.text: Agriculture is the science, practice and business of producing crops and livestock and of managing the soil, water, plants, animals and natural resources on which production depends. It includes fisheries, forestry, agroforestry and wildlife, and the steps after harvest: storage, processing, marketing and extension. It draws on biology, chemistry, physics, economics and social science. A farmer decides under weather, price and pest risk, so an agriculture graduate must understand both the biological system and the business around it. It is not only how to farm but how to produce food and other products sustainably and profitably.

sections.heading: How an agriculture degree is usually organised
sections.text: Names, lengths and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, universities award BSc or BAgric, usually after a programme that includes lectures, laboratories and supervised farm practice. Polytechnics under the National Board for Technical Education award ND and HND. Colleges of education under the National Commission for Colleges of Education award NCE. University degrees commonly take four years, but entry route and institution can change this. In the UK, a BSc usually takes three years, and sandwich programmes take longer. In Kenya and Ghana, bachelor’s degrees in agriculture commonly take four years. Master’s degrees usually take one to two years and end with a dissertation. Check current rules with your department.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually starts with foundations: the meaning, scope and history of agriculture; its importance to national economies; agricultural ecology, climate and land; soil formation and properties; soil water, conservation and erosion control; plant morphology and classification; plant physiology and growth; crop propagation and nursery practice; farm surveying and land measurement; and farm machinery and power. These give the vocabulary and physical basis for later work.

The core then moves through crop protection and crop production: weeds and their control; crop pests and their management; crop diseases and their management; crop nutrition and fertiliser use; cereal crop production; legume, root and tuber crop production; vegetable and fruit crop production; and pasture and forage crops. Animal science follows: anatomy and physiology; nutrition and feed formulation; breeding and genetics; reproduction and husbandry; livestock health and disease control; and poultry production. Fisheries and aquaculture, forestry, agroforestry and wildlife extend the range of production systems.

The farm business and rural context come next: agricultural economics and farm management; marketing and cooperatives; extension and rural sociology; post-harvest handling, storage and processing; and ethics, safety and regulation. Research methods and the final project teach you to frame a question, collect and analyse data, and report honestly. At master’s level, advanced crop physiology and stress biology, advanced plant and animal breeding, sustainable agriculture and natural resource management, and advanced research methods and dissertation deepen the same themes.

sections.heading: How to study agriculture
sections.text:
Study agriculture in three connected ways. First, learn the science: draw and label a plant, a soil profile or an animal organ, and explain each process in your own words. Second, do the practical work: laboratory tests, field identification, farm records, feed and fertiliser calculations, and safe handling of tools and chemicals. Third, connect biology to money and risk: for each crop or animal enterprise, ask what it costs, what it yields, what can go wrong and how the farmer would decide.

Use local examples, but check recommendations against your own country’s extension service, research institute or current label. Keep a field notebook. For calculations, write the units at every step and check the answer by a rough estimate. For projects, read original papers and official reports, not only summaries.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
The commonest mistake is to memorise definitions and lists without being able to explain a process or solve a practical problem. Students also skip practicals and then cannot identify a pest, a disease symptom, a weed or a soil type. In fertiliser and feed work, they mix units, ignore the nutrient content on the label, or forget to check the calculation. In recommendations, they copy one country’s practice as if it were universal; climate, soil, law and market differ.

Other errors are unsafe use of pesticides, poor farm records, and treating economics as an afterthought. In the final project, students plagiarise, use data without checking its source, or claim more than their results show. Keep raw data, cite every source, and state the limits of your study.

keyPoints: Agriculture is a science, a practice and a business, not only a set of farming techniques.
Degree names, lengths and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Learn each topic in three ways: scientific explanation, practical skill and economic decision.
Correct identification of soil, plant, pest, disease and weed problems comes before control.
Recommendations for fertiliser, feed, chemicals and breeds must fit local climate, soil, law and market.
Keep raw data and cite sources; a project is judged on honesty and method as well as results.

en.title: Agriculture: Meaning, Scope and History
en.short: What agriculture is, its branches, why farming differs, and the road from gathering to the Green Revolution.

sections.heading: What agriculture means
sections.text:
Agriculture is the deliberate cultivation of plants and the rearing of animals for food, fibre, fuel and other products. It is usually divided into branches: crop production (agronomy for field crops, horticulture for fruits, vegetables and ornamentals), livestock husbandry, forestry, fisheries and aquaculture (the farming of aquatic organisms), and agroforestry, which combines trees with crops or livestock on the same land.

These branches overlap. A mixed farm may keep cattle, grow maize and hold a woodlot, and the trees may shelter the crops.

sections.heading: Why farming is different
sections.text:
Farming differs from factory production because its raw material is alive. Output depends on biological growth, so a crop or an animal takes weeks, months or years and cannot be hurried at will. Farming is land-based, seasonal and weather-dependent, and exposed to pests, disease and price swings.

A factory can stop and restart a line. A farmer who misses a planting date or a breeding window loses the season. Much produce is also bulky and perishable, which shapes how it is sold and stored.

sections.heading: From gathering to settled farming
sections.text:
For most of history people hunted, fished and gathered wild plants. From roughly 10,000 years ago, in several regions independently, people began domesticating plants and animals. This first agricultural revolution allowed settled villages and food surpluses.

In West Africa, pearl millet, African rice and yam were domesticated locally. Early systems included shifting cultivation, where land is cropped and then rested, and nomadic pastoralism, where herds move to find pasture.

sections.heading: Later revolutions
sections.text:
The British Agricultural Revolution of the 18th century brought crop rotations, selective livestock breeding and enclosure, which turned common land into private farms. The 19th and 20th centuries added machinery, synthetic fertiliser and pesticides.

The Green Revolution of the 1960s spread semi-dwarf, high-yielding wheat and rice together with irrigation and fertiliser, raising yields sharply in Asia and Latin America. Critics note that it favoured farmers with land, water and capital and brought environmental costs; organic and conservation farming grew partly in response.

keyPoints: Agriculture is the deliberate growing of plants and rearing of animals for food, fibre and other products.
Its main branches are crop production, livestock, forestry, fisheries and agroforestry.
Farming differs from industry because production depends on living organisms, land, season and weather.
Domestication began about 10,000 years ago in several regions independently, including West Africa.
The British Agricultural Revolution of the 18th century introduced rotations, selective breeding and enclosure.
The Green Revolution of the 1960s raised cereal yields through high-yielding varieties, irrigation and fertiliser, with uneven benefits.

en.title: The Importance of Agriculture to National Economies
en.short: Agriculture’s roles in food, raw materials, jobs, exports, savings and industry, with African examples.

sections.heading: Food, materials and jobs
sections.text: Agriculture supplies food for households and raw materials for industry: cotton for textiles, cocoa for chocolate, oilseeds for cooking oil and hides for leather. It employs farmers, labourers, traders and processors. Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total value of final goods and services produced in a country in a year. In Nigeria, Ghana and Kenya, agriculture is a major employer and a significant part of GDP. The exact shares of jobs and output change with the year and the definition used, so check current figures from the national statistical office, the World Bank or the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). In these countries the share of workers in agriculture is often higher than its share of GDP, which points to low output per worker.

sections.heading: Export earnings and savings
sections.text: Export crops earn foreign exchange: cocoa in Ghana and Nigeria, tea and horticulture in Kenya. Foreign exchange is money in other currencies, used to pay for imports such as fuel, medicine and machinery. Export earnings can be taxed to fund public investment. Farm profits and rural savings can be deposited in banks and lent to other farmers or firms for investment in tools, irrigation or processing. Dependence on one or two commodities makes these earnings volatile when world prices fall, so many countries try to add value by processing before export.

sections.heading: Industry and trade links
sections.text: Agriculture links backward to fertiliser, seed, machinery, credit and extension advice, and forward to processing, transport, storage and retail. These linkages create demand and jobs outside the farm. A small case: a Kenyan tea factory buys green leaf from smallholders, pays wages, transports tea and exports it. The farmers spend their income on local goods, and the factory buys services, so spending spreads through the local economy. This spread is the multiplier effect. Trade matters because exports depend on world prices, transport costs and rules such as tariffs and quality standards.

keyPoints: Agriculture supplies food and raw materials such as cotton, cocoa and oilseeds.
It provides employment on farms and in processing, transport and trade.
Export crops earn foreign exchange, but dependence on few commodities is risky.
Farm profits and rural savings can finance investment.
Agriculture has backward links to inputs and forward links to processing and retail.
Shares of jobs and output change, so check current official statistics.

en.title: Agricultural Ecology, Climate and Land
en.short: How climate, soil and altitude decide what can be grown, and how farmers adapt.

sections.heading: What ecology means here
sections.text:
Agricultural ecology is the study of how the environment around a farm shapes what can be grown there. Six factors do most of the work. Temperature sets the rate of growth and the length of the growing season. Rainfall supplies water, and humidity controls how much water a plant loses through transpiration. Sunlight drives photosynthesis. Soil supplies nutrients, water and anchorage. Altitude matters mainly because it changes temperature.

These factors act together. A place with good rain but shallow, sandy soil still limits what a farmer can grow.

sections.heading: Climate and vegetation zones
sections.text:
West Africa is often divided, from south to north, into mangrove and rainforest, derived savanna, Guinea savanna, Sudan savanna, Sahel and desert. Rainfall decreases and the dry season lengthens as you move north, so the growing season shortens.

Worldwide, broad zones include tropical, subtropical, Mediterranean, temperate, continental, arid and polar. Each zone has a matching natural vegetation type, such as rainforest, savanna, grassland or desert scrub.

sections.heading: Altitude and soil
sections.text:
Air cools as it rises. In the lower atmosphere the average rate is about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m, called the environmental lapse rate. Example: a town at 200 m averages 28 °C. A highland site at 1,700 m is 1,500 m higher, so it is about 1.5 × 6.5 = 9.75 °C cooler, near 18 °C. This is why tropical highlands in Nigeria, Kenya and Ethiopia can grow temperate crops such as potatoes and wheat.

Deep, well drained soil holds more water that crops can use and more nutrients than shallow soil, and unlike waterlogged soil it lets roots get air, so it supports more crops.

sections.heading: How farmers adapt
sections.text: Farmers match crops to the zone. In dry savanna and Sahel they grow millet, sorghum and cowpea, choose early maturing varieties, plant on ridges, trap rainwater in planting pits and keep shelterbelts against wind. In the humid forest zone they grow cassava, plantain, cocoa and oil palm, often under agroforestry with trees. On slopes they terrace and use contour strips. Where land is scarce, they use fadama, the low-lying moist valley land, for dry-season vegetables.

keyPoints: Temperature, rainfall, humidity, sunlight, soil and altitude together decide which crops suit a place.
In West Africa, rainfall decreases and the dry season lengthens from the coast northward, so the growing season shortens.
Air cools about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m of altitude, so tropical highlands can grow temperate crops.
Deep, well drained, fertile soil supports more crops than shallow or waterlogged soil.
Farmers adapt by choosing suitable crops and varieties, and by using water harvesting, mulching, terracing and agroforestry.
Climate zones are broad patterns; local soil and slope can change what is possible on one farm.

en.title: Soil Formation and Soil Properties
en.short: How soil forms, its horizons, and how texture, structure, pH and CEC affect roots, water and nutrients.

sections.heading: Forming factors and profile
sections.text:
Soil forms from weathered parent rock plus organic matter. Parent rock supplies minerals. Climate, mainly rainfall and temperature, drives weathering and decay. Organisms such as roots, microbes and earthworms mix soil and recycle nutrients. Relief affects drainage and erosion: slopes lose soil, flat land holds deeper soil. Time allows horizons to develop.

A profile is a vertical section. Horizons are layers: O litter; A topsoil with humus and roots; E leached pale layer; B subsoil where leached clay and iron accumulate; C weathered rock; R bedrock. Not every soil has all horizons.

sections.heading: Physical properties
sections.text: Texture is the proportion of sand, silt and clay. Sandy soil drains fast but holds little water or nutrients. Clay holds water and nutrients but drains slowly and can resist roots. Loam is balanced. Structure is how particles form aggregates; good structure gives roots and air space. Porosity is the fraction of soil volume that is pore space, holding air and water. Colour is only a clue: dark often means organic matter, red or yellow iron oxides, grey waterlogging. Organic matter improves structure, porosity and water holding.

sections.heading: Chemical properties
sections.text:
Soil pH measures acidity or alkalinity from 0 to 14. Many crops grow best near pH 6 to 7, where nutrients are most available. Cation exchange capacity (CEC) is the soil’s ability to hold exchangeable cations such as calcium, magnesium and potassium. It is measured in cmol(+)/kg, centimoles of charge per kilogram. Clay and organic matter raise CEC, helping retain nutrients against leaching.

Worked example: exchangeable Ca 8, Mg 3, K 1, Na 0.5 and acidic H + Al 2 cmol(+)/kg. CEC = 8 + 3 + 1 + 0.5 + 2 = 14.5 cmol(+)/kg. Base saturation = (8 + 3 + 1 + 0.5) ÷ 14.5 × 100 = 86.2%. High base saturation means most exchange sites hold nutrient bases, not acidity.

keyPoints: Soil forms from parent rock under climate, organisms, relief and time.
Horizons are O, A, E, B, C and R layers in a profile.
Texture is sand, silt and clay proportions; structure is aggregation; porosity is pore space.
pH controls nutrient availability; CEC is the capacity to hold exchangeable cations.
CEC = sum of exchangeable cations in cmol(+)/kg; base saturation = base cations ÷ CEC × 100.
Organic matter improves structure, porosity, water holding and CEC.

en.title: Soil Water, Conservation and Erosion Control
en.short: Soil water forms, moisture measurement, erosion types and control methods on African farms.

sections.heading: Soil water forms
sections.text: Soil water has three forms. Gravitational water fills large pores and drains under gravity after rain. Capillary water is held in small pores by capillary forces and is the main water available to roots. Hygroscopic water is a thin film bound tightly to soil particles and is unavailable to plants. Water holding capacity is the water a soil can retain; field capacity is the water left after gravitational drainage. Sandy soils hold less than clayey soils.

sections.heading: Infiltration and measurement
sections.text: Infiltration is the entry of water through the soil surface. Percolation is its downward movement through soil. The gravimetric method measures moisture: weigh a moist sample, dry it at 105 degrees Celsius to constant mass, then reweigh. Gravimetric moisture = (wet mass − dry mass) ÷ dry mass × 100. If wet soil is 120 g and dry soil is 100 g, water is 20 g, so moisture is 20 ÷ 100 × 100 = 20 per cent. Volumetric moisture = gravimetric moisture × bulk density ÷ density of water. With bulk density 1.3 g/cm³, it is 0.20 × 1.3 = 0.26, or 26 per cent.

sections.heading: Erosion causes and types
sections.text: Erosion is the detachment and removal of soil by water or wind. Causes include clearing vegetation, overgrazing, poor tillage, steep slopes, intense rainfall and compaction that reduces infiltration. Water erosion begins with splash, then sheet erosion, rills and gullies. Wind erosion lifts loose dry particles from bare sandy soils. Erosion reduces soil depth, nutrients and water holding capacity.

sections.heading: Control on African farms
sections.text: Control methods suit local slopes, rainfall and soil. Terracing builds steps on steep slopes to slow runoff. Contour ridging runs ridges across the slope, not up and down it. Mulching covers the soil with crop residues to protect it from raindrops and reduce evaporation. Cover crops grow low plants that shield the soil between main crops. Alley cropping plants food crops between hedgerows of trees or shrubs that trap soil and add organic matter. Check local advice.

keyPoints: Gravitational water drains, capillary water is available to plants, and hygroscopic water is unavailable.
Water holding capacity and field capacity describe how much water a soil retains after drainage.
Infiltration is entry at the surface; percolation is downward movement.
Gravimetric moisture = (wet mass − dry mass) ÷ dry mass × 100; volumetric moisture = gravimetric moisture × bulk density ÷ density of water.
Erosion by water moves from splash to sheet, rill and gully; wind erosion affects bare dry soil.
Terracing, contour ridging, mulching, cover crops and alley cropping reduce erosion on African farms, with local advice.

en.title: Plant Morphology and Classification
en.short: The main plant organs, the classification hierarchy, monocots and dicots, and the practical crop groups.

sections.heading: Organs and functions
sections.text: Roots anchor the plant, absorb water and mineral salts, and may store food; root hairs increase the absorbing surface. Stems support leaves and flowers, carry water and minerals upward in xylem and sugars in phloem, and may store food. Leaves carry out most photosynthesis; stomata allow gas exchange, and transpiration pulls water up. Flowers are reproductive shoots: stamens make pollen, and the carpel encloses the ovules in its ovary. After fertilisation the ovary becomes the fruit, which protects and disperses seeds. A seed contains an embryo, stored food and a seed coat.

sections.heading: Classification hierarchy
sections.text: Classification uses a hierarchy: kingdom, division (phylum in animals), class, order, family, genus, species. A crop species has a two-part name, genus then species, for example Zea mays for maize. Cultivars and varieties sit below species. Groupings are revised as evidence changes, so check a current flora or database.

sections.heading: Monocots and dicots
sections.text: Flowering plants are often split into monocotyledons and dicotyledons. Monocots have one cotyledon (seed leaf), parallel leaf veins, scattered stem vascular bundles and fibrous roots; floral parts usually in threes. Dicots have two cotyledons, net-like veins, vascular bundles in a ring and usually a taproot; floral parts usually in fours or fives. Exceptions exist, so treat these as useful guides.

sections.heading: Crop groups
sections.text: Cereals are grasses grown for grain, such as maize, rice and sorghum. Legumes are grown for pods and seeds and often fix nitrogen with rhizobia (soil bacteria), as cowpea does. Root and tuber crops store food underground: cassava and sweet potato are roots; yam and potato are tubers. Vegetables are grown for leaves, stems, roots, flowers or fruits. Fruit crops are grown for fruit. Fibre crops include cotton (seed fibre) and jute (stem fibre). Beverage crops include tea, coffee and cocoa. A farmer in Oyo State, Nigeria, may plant maize, a monocot cereal, beside cowpea, a dicot legume.

keyPoints: Roots absorb and anchor; stems support and transport; leaves photosynthesise; flowers reproduce; fruits protect and disperse seeds; seeds contain an embryo with stored food.
Classification runs kingdom, division, class, order, family, genus, species.
Monocots have one cotyledon, parallel veins and fibrous roots; dicots have two cotyledons, net veins and usually a taproot.
Cereals are grasses grown for grain; legumes are grown for pods and seeds and often fix nitrogen.
Root and tuber crops store food underground; vegetables, fruits, fibre and beverage crops are grouped by their harvested product.
Use two-part genus and species names, and check current sources because plant classification changes.

en.title: Plant Physiology and Growth
en.short: Photosynthesis, respiration, water and mineral transport, germination, hormones and flowering.

sections.heading: Energy capture
sections.text:
Photosynthesis makes sugars from carbon dioxide and water in chloroplasts: 6CO2 + 6H2O gives C6H12O6 + 6O2. Light reactions in the thylakoid membranes split water and release oxygen; the Calvin cycle then fixes CO2 using ATP and NADPH. C3, C4 and CAM plants differ in carbon fixation and water use.

Respiration releases that energy: C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O plus ATP. Aerobic respiration in mitochondria powers growth; anaerobic respiration in waterlogged roots makes ethanol and damages tissue.

sections.heading: Water and minerals
sections.text:
Water rises in the xylem mainly by transpiration pull. Evaporation through leaf stomata lowers water potential, and cohesion between water molecules pulls the column up. Transpiration cools the leaf and moves nutrients, but excess loss wilts the plant; guard cells close stomata to save water.

Translocation is sugar movement in the phloem from sources (mature leaves) to sinks (growing tips, roots, fruits) by pressure flow. Mineral uptake is active: roots absorb ions such as nitrate and potassium against a gradient using energy, often aided by mycorrhizal fungi.

sections.heading: Germination and growth
sections.text:
Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Imbibition swells the seed, enzymes break down stored starch, and the radicle emerges first. Growth phases are lag, log (rapid) and decline.

Hormones steer growth: auxin for elongation and rooting, gibberellin for stem elongation and germination, cytokinin for cell division, abscisic acid for dormancy and stomatal closure, ethylene for ripening.

sections.heading: Environment and flowering
sections.text:
Day length (photoperiod) controls flowering: short-day plants flower when nights exceed a critical length, long-day plants when nights are short. Temperature acts through vernalisation (cold needed to flower) and heat accumulation.

Growing degree days sum daily heat above a base temperature; with base 10 °C, daily means of 22, 24 and 20 °C give (12 + 14 + 10) = 36 GDD. Moisture stress delays flowering and maturity.

keyPoints: Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O gives C6H12O6 + 6O2; respiration reverses it to release ATP.
Transpiration pull, driven by evaporation and cohesion, lifts water up the xylem.
Translocation moves sugars in the phloem from source to sink by pressure flow.
Mineral uptake is active and needs energy, often helped by mycorrhizae.
Germination requires water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.
Growing degree days = sum of (daily mean temperature − base temperature).

en.title: Crop Propagation and Nursery Practice
en.short: It compares seed and vegetative propagation and covers seed quality, nursery layout, media, hardening and transplanting.

sections.heading: Seed versus vegetative
sections.text: Sexual propagation raises plants from seed formed by fertilisation. Seedlings vary genetically, which suits breeding but not uniform crops. Seed is cheap and easy to store. Vegetative propagation uses plant parts, so offspring are clones and true to type. Cuttings are detached stem, leaf or root pieces that grow into new plants. Layering roots a stem while still attached to the parent. Grafting joins a scion (shoot) to a rootstock; budding inserts one bud under the bark. Division splits clumps; tissue culture grows shoots in sterile laboratory media. Vegetative methods need skill and can spread disease, but shorten time to fruiting.

sections.heading: Seed testing and dormancy
sections.text: Seed testing checks purity, moisture and germination. Viability is the proportion of seed alive and able to germinate. Germination percentage = (normal seedlings ÷ seeds tested) × 100. For example, 320 normal seedlings from 400 seeds give 320 ÷ 400 × 100 = 80%. Dormancy is when a viable seed fails to germinate under favourable conditions. Causes include a hard seed coat, immature embryo or chemical inhibitors. Treatments include scarification (breaking the coat), stratification (moist cold) and soaking. Follow the species’ known treatment.

sections.heading: Nursery layout and media
sections.text: A nursery needs beds or containers, paths, water, shade, a potting shed, windbreaks and clean tools. Layout should allow easy movement and drainage. Potting media must hold moisture yet drain freely and be free of pests. Common mixtures use soil, sand, compost or coco peat. Sterilise reused media or use clean commercial mix. Sow at the recommended depth, label the bed and thin overcrowded seedlings.

sections.heading: Hardening and transplanting
sections.text: Hardening off gradually prepares seedlings for field conditions. Reduce water and shade, and expose plants to more sun over about a week. Transplant when seedlings have true leaves and a firm root ball. Water before lifting, keep roots covered, set the seedling at its original depth and firm the soil. Water after planting and give temporary shade. Avoid hot midday sun.

keyPoints: Sexual propagation uses seed and gives genetic variation; vegetative propagation uses plant parts and gives clones.
Cuttings, layering, grafting, budding, division and tissue culture are vegetative methods.
Viability is the proportion of live seed; germination percentage = (normal seedlings ÷ seeds tested) × 100.
Dormancy is a viable seed failing to germinate under favourable conditions; treat with scarification, stratification or soaking as the species requires.
Nursery layout needs beds, paths, water, shade, windbreak and clean tools; potting media must drain yet hold moisture.
Harden seedlings by reducing water and shade before transplanting, then water and firm the soil.

en.title: Farm Surveying and Land Measurement
en.short: Using chain, tape, compass, level and pegs to measure and lay out farm land, with area and contour basics.

sections.heading: Tools and layout
sections.text: A chain or tape measures distance along a straight line. Ranging poles mark the line so it stays straight. Pegs mark stations and corners. A compass gives bearings, the clockwise angle of a line from north, so you can record direction. A level on a tripod with a staff measures height difference. To lay out a plot, set a baseline, mark corners with pegs, measure offsets at right angles to the baseline, and record bearings and distances in a field book.

sections.heading: Area of plots
sections.text: For regular shapes use formulas: rectangle area = length × width; triangle area = ½ × base × height; trapezium area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height. For an irregular plot, divide it into triangles and trapezia, or measure offsets from a baseline. Worked example: baseline 40 m, offsets at equal intervals of 10 m are 0, 4, 6, 5 and 0 m. Trapezoidal rule: area = 10 × [(0+0)÷2 + 4 + 6 + 5] = 10 × 15 = 150 m². Check: 150 m² = 0.015 ha.

sections.heading: Levelling and contours
sections.text: A level finds differences in height. Take a backsight on a point of known level and a foresight on the new point. Height difference = backsight − foresight. Add this to the known level to get the new reduced level. A contour is a line joining points of equal height. Contour maps guide drainage, irrigation and contour ploughing, which runs across the slope along the contour lines to slow runoff. Levelling a field makes it flat for even water spread.

sections.heading: Units and titles
sections.text: Area is measured in square metres (m²). 1 hectare = 10,000 m². 1 acre ≈ 4,046.86 m², so 1 hectare ≈ 2.47 acres. Local units such as the plot vary widely; in Nigeria, plot size and land titles differ by state and layout. Confirm current official units and title documents with a registered surveyor or the land registry before buying or registering land.

keyPoints: A chain or tape measures distance, ranging poles keep a line straight, and pegs mark stations and corners.
A compass records bearings measured clockwise from north, and a level with a staff measures height difference.
Rectangle area = length × width; triangle area = ½ × base × height; trapezium area = ½ × (a + b) × h.
For irregular plots, use offsets and the trapezoidal rule: area = h × [(first + last) ÷ 2 + sum of middle offsets].
Height difference = backsight − foresight; contours join points of equal height and guide drainage and ploughing.
1 hectare = 10,000 m² and 1 acre ≈ 4,046.86 m²; confirm local plot sizes and land titles with official sources.

en.title: Farm Machinery and Power
en.short: Tillage, planting, spraying and harvesting implements, tractor systems, safety and machinery cost.

sections.heading: Power sources and tractor systems
sections.text:
Farm power comes from human labour, animals, engines and electricity. A tractor has an engine, transmission, hydraulic system, power take-off (PTO) and three-point linkage. The PTO drives rotary implements; the linkage lifts mounted ones.

Hitching may be mounted, semi-mounted or trailed. Pull loads from the drawbar, not the top link. Use a roll-over protective structure (ROPS), seat belt, guards and PTO shields. Keep bystanders away.

sections.heading: Tillage and planting
sections.text:
Tillage is the mechanical manipulation of soil. Primary tillage (ploughing) breaks and inverts soil. Secondary tillage (harrowing, ridging) breaks clods and levels the seedbed. Implements are pulled by draft (the pulling force) or driven by the PTO. Hand tools include the hoe, cutlass and dibber. Animal-drawn ploughs and harrows suit small farms.

Planting implements meter seed at a set spacing and depth. Calibrate a seed drill or planter by collecting seed over a measured distance and comparing with the target. Check depth and blockage.

sections.heading: Spraying, harvesting and processing
sections.text:
Sprayers have a tank, pump, pressure regulator and nozzles. Nozzle size, pressure and speed set the application rate. Calibrate before spraying, check for drift (spray carried by wind), wear personal protective equipment (PPE) and follow the label.

Harvesting cuts the crop; threshing separates grain from the ear; cleaning removes chaff. A combine harvester does these together. Processing includes shelling maize, milling grain and drying. Clean, lubricate, sharpen and store machines.

sections.heading: Selection, maintenance and cost
sections.text:
Choose implements to match farm size, soil, crop, power and spare parts. Too wide overloads the tractor; too narrow wastes time. Maintain by cleaning, lubricating and replacing worn parts.

Cost has fixed costs (depreciation, interest, shelter, insurance) and variable costs (fuel, repairs, labour). Example: tractor price 12,000,000 units, life 10 years, salvage 2,000,000. Straight-line depreciation = (12,000,000 − 2,000,000) ÷ 10 = 1,000,000 yearly. At 1,000 hours yearly, that is 1,000 per hour. Fuel use is 6 litres per hour; at 500 per litre that is 3,000 per hour. Add repairs 500 and labour 1,500 per hour. Total = 1,000 + 3,000 + 500 + 1,500 = 6,000 per hour. If a plough covers 0.5 hectare per hour, cost = 6,000 ÷ 0.5 = 12,000 per hectare.

keyPoints: Farm power comes from human, animal, mechanical and electrical sources; a tractor’s PTO drives rotary implements and its three-point linkage lifts mounted ones.
Primary tillage breaks and inverts soil; secondary tillage breaks clods and levels the seedbed.
Calibrate planters and sprayers before use, and wear PPE when handling pesticides.
Match implement width and power to farm size, soil and crop, and keep ROPS, guards and PTO shields in place.
Straight-line annual depreciation = (purchase price − salvage value) ÷ useful life.
Cost per hour = fixed cost per hour + variable cost per hour; cost per hectare = cost per hour ÷ area covered per hour.

en.title: Weeds and Their Control
en.short: Weed definition, classification, competition, spread and preventive to chemical control.

sections.heading: Weed definition and types
sections.text: A weed is an unwanted plant interfering with a crop or land use. Weeds are classified by life cycle as annual (one season), biennial (two seasons) and perennial (several years, often spreading by roots or rhizomes). By morphology they are broadleaf (dicotyledonous, net veins), grasses (monocotyledonous, narrow leaves, parallel veins) and sedges (grass-like monocots, often triangular solid stems; 'sedges have edges').

sections.heading: Competition and spread
sections.text: Weeds compete with crops for light, water, nutrients and space. Early competition is often most damaging because young crops are small. Weeds can also host pests and diseases, raise harvest costs and reduce produce quality. They spread by seed and vegetative parts such as rhizomes, tubers and stolons. Wind, water, animals, machinery, contaminated seed and manure move them; seeds survive in the soil seed bank for years.

sections.heading: Control methods
sections.text: Preventive control stops introduction: clean seed, clean machinery, quarantine and sanitation. Cultural control makes the crop more competitive: crop rotation, timely planting, closer spacing, mulching, cover crops and stale seedbeds. Mechanical control uses hand pulling, hoeing, mowing and tillage. Biological control uses specific natural enemies such as insects or pathogens; it needs safety testing and patience. Integrated weed management combines methods.

sections.heading: Herbicides and dosage
sections.text:
Herbicides are grouped by mode of action, the way they kill plants: synthetic auxins (2,4-D, Group 4), ALS inhibitors (sulfonylureas, Group 2), photosystem II inhibitors (atrazine, Group 5) and EPSPS inhibitors (glyphosate, Group 9). Selective herbicides injure weeds more than the crop; non-selective ones kill most plants. Selectivity depends on crop and weed biology, dose, timing, placement and formulation. Read the label, wear protective clothing, follow re-entry and pre-harvest intervals, avoid drift and dispose safely.

Worked example: label rate 1.5 kg active ingredient per hectare. For 0.8 ha, active ingredient = 1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2 kg. With a 60% wettable powder, product = 1.2 ÷ 0.60 = 2.0 kg. Check: 2.0 × 0.60 = 1.2 kg active ingredient.

keyPoints: A weed is an unwanted plant that interferes with a crop or land use.
Life cycle classes are annual, biennial and perennial; morphology classes are broadleaf, grass and sedge.
Weeds compete for light, water, nutrients and space and spread by seed and vegetative parts.
Integrated weed management combines preventive, cultural, mechanical, biological and chemical methods.
Herbicides are grouped by mode of action; selectivity depends on crop and weed biology, dose, timing, placement and formulation.
Product needed = (active ingredient rate × area) ÷ product concentration; always follow the label and wear protective clothing.

en.title: Crop Pests and Their Management
en.short: Identifying African crop pests and managing them through integrated pest management.

sections.heading: Insect and mite pests
sections.text:
Insect pests feed in different ways, and the damage shows it. Chewing larvae such as the fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda), which spread across Africa from 2016, leave window-pane holes and ragged whorls with frass in maize. Stem borers tunnel into stems and cause dead heart, where the central shoot dries. Sucking pests such as aphids and whitefly cause leaf curling, honeydew and sooty mould.

Mites are tiny sap feeders, not insects. The cassava green mite gives yellow speckling and stunting, and spider mites leave fine webbing.

sections.heading: Nematodes, rodents and birds
sections.text:
Nematodes are microscopic roundworms. Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne species) invade roots and cause galls, so tomato and okra wilt in the heat and grow poorly.

The multimammate mouse (Mastomys natalensis) is a major rodent pest: it cuts young tillers, gnaws cobs and leaves runways and droppings. The red-billed quelea (Quelea quelea) moves in large flocks and strips sorghum, millet and rice panicles, leaving empty husks and grain on the ground.

sections.heading: Integrated pest management
sections.text:
Integrated pest management (IPM) combines methods and uses chemicals only when monitoring shows they are needed. Monitor by scouting and pheromone traps, then compare counts with an action threshold, the pest level at which control pays. If the threshold is 20 percent of plants damaged and you inspect 50 plants, act when 10 or more are damaged (0.20 × 50 = 10).

Cultural control includes rotation, cereal-legume intercropping, early planting and destroying residues. Resistant varieties are another non-chemical tool. Biological control uses predators, parasitoids and pathogens such as Bacillus thuringiensis.

sections.heading: Pesticides and safety
sections.text:
Pesticides are classified by target (insecticide, acaricide, nematicide, rodenticide), by mode of action (contact or systemic) and by chemical group (pyrethroids, organophosphates, neonicotinoids). Rotate groups to slow resistance.

Apply the label dose with a calibrated knapsack sprayer, at the right crop stage, and avoid flowering to protect bees. Wear the protective equipment stated on the label, respect the pre-harvest interval, never spray into the wind, and follow national registration rules, such as NAFDAC in Nigeria.

keyPoints: Match the pest group to its damage signs: chewing, sucking, galls, cut stems or stripped panicles.
IPM combines cultural, biological and resistant-variety methods, with chemicals as a last resort.
Act on an action threshold from monitoring, not on a fixed calendar.
Threshold count = threshold proportion × number of plants inspected.
Classify pesticides by target, mode of action and chemical group, and rotate groups to slow resistance.
Follow label dose, protective equipment, pre-harvest interval and national registration.

en.title: Crop Diseases and Their Management
en.short: Causes of crop disease, disease cycles, spread, symptoms and integrated control methods.

sections.heading: Causes of disease
sections.text: Plant disease is harmful change caused by a pathogen or environment. Fungi grow as threads and cause mildews, rusts, wilts and rots. Bacteria are single-celled and cause soft rots, wilts and leaf spots. Viruses multiply inside living cells and cause mosaic, mottle and stunting. Nematodes are small worm-like animals that damage roots and cause galls. Physiological disorders have no pathogen and do not spread; examples are sunscald and blossom end rot, linked to poor calcium movement into fruit under water stress.

sections.heading: Disease cycle and spread
sections.text: The disease cycle is how a pathogen survives, infects, colonises, reproduces and spreads. Inoculum is the material that starts infection, such as spores or infected cuttings. A symptom is the plant’s visible response, such as a lesion or wilt. A sign is the pathogen itself, such as mould or spores. Disease needs a susceptible host, a virulent pathogen and favourable environment, often called the disease triangle. Sources include soil, seed, debris, weeds and vectors. Spread is by wind, water, soil, seed, tools and insects.

sections.heading: Control principles
sections.text: Control uses integrated management. Quarantine keeps new pathogens out of a country or region by inspecting and restricting plant material. Clean seed and planting material are free from the pathogen; certified seed is tested. Resistant varieties carry genes that limit infection or damage. Cultural practice includes crop rotation, removing infected debris, spacing for airflow, avoiding overhead irrigation and roguing, which means removing diseased plants. Biological control uses living agents such as antagonistic fungi or bacteria. Fungicides kill or inhibit fungi; they give little or no control of bacteria and viruses, and misuse can lead to resistance.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Case: a farmer in Kaduna, Nigeria, sees cassava with mosaic leaves and stunting. Cassava mosaic disease is caused by viruses and spread by whitefly and infected cuttings. The farmer should destroy diseased plants, use certified virus-free cuttings, plant resistant varieties and manage whiteflies. Fungicide cannot cure the virus.

keyPoints: Plant diseases are caused by fungi, bacteria, viruses, nematodes or non-infectious physiological disorders.
Symptoms are plant responses; signs are the pathogen or its structures.
Disease develops when a susceptible host, virulent pathogen and favourable environment meet.
Inoculum survives in soil, seed, debris, weeds and vectors, and spreads by wind, water, tools and insects.
Integrated control uses quarantine, clean seed, resistant varieties, cultural practice and biological agents.
Fungicides control fungi, not bacteria or viruses, and misuse can cause resistance.

en.title: Crop Nutrition and Fertiliser Use
en.short: Essential nutrients, deficiency signs, fertiliser types, labels, placement, manure and rate calculations.

sections.heading: Essential nutrients
sections.text: Plants need 17 essential elements. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from air and water. The rest come mainly from soil: macronutrients nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg) and sulphur (S), and micronutrients iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), zinc (Zn), copper (Cu), boron (B), molybdenum (Mo), chlorine (Cl) and nickel (Ni). N builds proteins and chlorophyll; P supports energy transfer and roots; K regulates water and enzymes. Deficiency signs vary: N gives pale older leaves; P dark or purple older leaves; K scorched older leaf margins; Mg yellowing between veins on older leaves; Fe yellowing between veins on young leaves. Confirm with soil or tissue tests.

sections.heading: Fertilisers and labels
sections.text: Fertilisers are straight (one nutrient), compound or complex (two or more chemically combined), or blends (mixed granules). Organic sources include manure, compost and green manure. Labels commonly give N-P-K, with P as P2O5 and K as K2O; check the local label because conventions differ. A 20-10-10 contains 20% N, 10% P2O5 and 10% K2O by mass. Placement and timing affect recovery: broadcast and incorporate before planting, band beside rows, side-dress during growth, or fertigate. Keep fertiliser away from seed and roots. Split nitrogen applications to reduce leaching and volatilisation. Apply well-rotted manure or compost before planting; they supply some nutrients and organic matter but are variable, so test them.

sections.heading: Rate calculation
sections.text: From a soil test or field trial, the recommendation is usually given as kg of nutrient per hectare. Product needed = nutrient required ÷ fraction of nutrient in the product. Example: a soil test recommends 60 kg N/ha. Urea is 46% N, so urea needed = 60 ÷ 0.46 = 130.4 kg/ha. Check: 130.4 × 0.46 = 60.0 kg N. If using a 20-10-10 compound to supply the same N, product = 60 ÷ 0.20 = 300 kg/ha; this also supplies 300 × 0.10 = 30 kg P2O5/ha and 30 kg K2O/ha. For a field trial, response = yield with fertiliser − yield without. Convert plot yields to per hectare before comparing. Confirm rates with local extension advice.

keyPoints: Plants need 17 essential elements, including macronutrients and micronutrients.
Deficiency symptoms suggest a nutrient but need soil or tissue confirmation.
N-P-K labels commonly show N, P as P2O5 and K as K2O.
Product needed = nutrient required ÷ fraction of nutrient in the product.
Place fertiliser away from seed and split nitrogen applications.
Manure and compost supply nutrients and organic matter but vary, so test them.

en.title: Cereal Crop Production
en.short: Agronomy of maize, rice, sorghum, millet and wheat, with spacing, fertiliser, field problems and grain storage.

sections.heading: Crop and variety choice
sections.text:
Cereals are grasses grown for edible grain. Africa’s main cereals are maize, rice, sorghum, millet and wheat. Maize and rice yield well where water and nutrients are adequate. Sorghum and millet tolerate heat and drought. Wheat is mainly a cool-season crop for highlands or irrigation. Match crop to rainfall, soil and market.

A variety is a named, genetically distinct type. Improved open-pollinated varieties can be saved for seed; hybrid seed must be bought each season. Use certified seed recommended for your area, and check current lists from extension or national research institutes.

sections.heading: Land, planting and spacing
sections.text:
Prepare a weed-free seedbed, or use conservation tillage, leaving crop residues, where erosion is a risk. Plant when soil moisture is adequate and the rains are established. Planting dates vary by crop, variety and place, so follow local recommendations. Wheat is sown in the cool season.

Spacing sets plant population. For maize at 75 cm between rows and 25 cm within rows:
area per plant = 0.75 × 0.25 = 0.1875 m²
plants per hectare = 10,000 ÷ 0.1875 = 53,333
Check this against seed rate and germination.

Fertiliser advice should come from soil tests and local recommendations. Cereals mainly need nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Split nitrogen (apply it in doses) for maize and rice. Urea is about 46% N, so 60 kg N/ha needs 60 ÷ 0.46 = 130 kg urea/ha.

sections.heading: Field problems and harvest
sections.text:
Weeds compete early, so weed before the canopy closes. Important problems include fall armyworm in maize, striga in maize, sorghum and millet, rice blast, birds and rodents. Scout fields and use integrated management: resistant varieties, timely planting, rotation, and approved pesticides only as labelled.

Harvest at physiological maturity, when grains are hard and moisture has fallen. Dry grain before storage. Maize is often dried to about 12 to 13% moisture, but check local standards. Damp grain grows moulds that can produce aflatoxin, a poison. Insects and rodents also cause loss. Clean and dry the store, use hermetic (airtight) bags or sealed silos, and inspect regularly. Thresh and clean grain promptly.

keyPoints: Match cereal crop and certified variety to rainfall, soil, season and market.
Plant population per hectare = 10,000 ÷ (row spacing × within-row spacing), with spacings in metres.
Fertiliser rates should follow soil tests; urea kg = required N kg ÷ 0.46.
Scout for fall armyworm, striga, rice blast, birds and rodents, and use integrated management.
Harvest at physiological maturity and dry grain before storage to limit mould and aflatoxin.
Clean, dry, sealed storage and regular inspection reduce insect, rodent and mould losses.

en.title: Legume, Root and Tuber Crop Production
en.short: Grain legumes and root/tuber crops: planting material, spacing, weeding, harvest, storage and processing.

sections.heading: Grain legumes
sections.text: Grain legumes are grown for dry seed. Cowpea, groundnut and bambara nut are often sown from seed saved from a healthy crop; soybean seed is fragile and should be fresh, and in a field new to soybean the seed is inoculated with the right rhizobia. Rhizobia are soil bacteria that form nodules and fix nitrogen. Spacing depends on variety and whether the crop is sole or intercropped, so use local recommendations. Keep the crop weed-free early; weed shallowly because groundnut pegs and legume roots are easily damaged. Harvest when pods or shells are mature and dry, before shattering or mould. Dry seed well before storage. Cowpea is attacked by bruchids, groundnut can be contaminated with aflatoxin if dried poorly, and soybean seed loses viability quickly.

sections.heading: Roots and tubers
sections.text: Root and tuber crops are propagated from vegetative material: cassava from stem cuttings, yam from whole small tubers or cut setts, sweet potato from vine cuttings, and cocoyam from corms or cormels. Use clean, healthy planting material. Spacing and plant density vary with species and variety. Weeding is critical early, and yam vines are usually staked. Harvest by lifting carefully to avoid bruising. Cassava, yam, sweet potato and cocoyam are bulky and perishable. Cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides, so it must be processed by grating, fermenting, pressing and drying or cooking. Yam and cocoyam need ventilated storage; sweet potato needs curing and cool storage; cocoyam is cooked to reduce acridity.

sections.heading: Spacing example
sections.text: A field is 20 m × 25 m = 500 m². At 0.5 m × 0.2 m, each stand occupies 0.1 m². 500 ÷ 0.1 = 5,000 stands. Add 10% for gaps: 5,000 × 1.1 = 5,500 stands. Check: 5,000 × 0.1 = 500 m², which matches the field area; the extra 500 stands are spare for replanting gaps.

keyPoints: Grain legumes are grown for dry seed; inoculate soybean seed with rhizobia in new fields.
Use fresh, healthy seed or vegetative planting material; spacing follows local recommendations.
Weed early and shallowly; groundnut pegs and legume roots damage easily.
Harvest legumes when mature and dry; dry seed well to limit aflatoxin, and protect stored cowpea from bruchids.
Cassava must be processed to reduce cyanogenic glycosides; yam, sweet potato and cocoyam need careful curing or ventilated storage.
Plant population = field area ÷ area per stand; add a gap allowance, e.g. 500 m² ÷ 0.1 m² = 5,000 stands, then × 1.1 = 5,500.

en.title: Vegetable and Fruit Crop Production
en.short: Production of African vegetables and fruits, irrigation, pruning, maturity indices and careful handling.

sections.heading: Vegetables
sections.text: Tomato, pepper and okra are grown for their fruits or pods; amaranth for leaves; onion for bulbs. They need well-drained soil, full sun and steady moisture. Many of these vegetables have shallow roots, so irrigation must be regular but not waterlogging. Drip or furrow irrigation is common; avoid wetting leaves where disease is a risk. Mulch conserves water. The critical stages are flowering and fruit set for tomato, pepper and okra, leaf growth for amaranth, and bulb enlargement for onion. Stop watering onion near maturity so bulbs cure well. A small case: Aisha in Kano mulches her tomato beds and waters at flowering, so the plants suffer less flower drop in dry spells.

sections.heading: Fruits
sections.text: Citrus, mango, banana and plantain are perennial; pineapple is a herbaceous perennial grown as an annual crop. Staking supports weak or top-heavy plants. Banana and plantain are propped with forked poles when bunches form. Pruning removes dead, diseased or crossing branches and opens the canopy of citrus and mango to light and air. Avoid heavy pruning in one season. Pineapple needs little pruning apart from removing slips and suckers, which can be used as planting material. Good airflow reduces fungal disease.

sections.heading: Maturity and handling
sections.text: A maturity index is a visible or measured sign that a crop is ready. Tomato: colour and firmness. Pepper: full colour and firmness. Okra: tender pod before it becomes fibrous. Amaranth: leaves before flowering. Onion: tops fall and neck dries. Citrus: colour, size and juice content. Mango: shoulder fill and pulp colour. Banana and plantain: angular ridges fill and colour changes. Pineapple: flat eyes, colour and aroma. Harvest in the cool of the day with sharp tools leaving a short stalk where useful. Do not drop fruit. Shade it at once, remove field heat (warmth trapped in the crop), sort out damaged units and pack in ventilated crates. Keep ethylene-producing mango and banana away from ethylene-sensitive produce such as leafy vegetables where possible. These steps reduce bruising, rotting and water loss.

keyPoints: Vegetables need steady moisture; irrigate at flowering and fruit set, and at bulb enlargement for onion, without waterlogging.
Staking and propping support weak plants and heavy banana or plantain bunches, while pruning opens citrus and mango canopies.
A maturity index is a sign of readiness, such as tomato colour, tender okra, or a drying onion neck.
Harvest in the cool of the day with sharp tools and avoid bruising or dropping produce.
Shade, sort, ventilate and cool produce quickly to reduce spoilage.
Varieties, pests and market standards vary by place, so check local extension advice.

en.title: Pasture and Forage Crops
en.short: Rangeland, pasture and forage types, establishment, stocking, grazing, hay, silage and quality.

sections.heading: Terms and classes
sections.text:
Rangeland is natural grassland, shrubland or savanna grazed extensively, usually not sown or fertilised. Natural pasture is native or long-established vegetation grazed in place. Improved pasture is sown with species and managed with fertiliser, weed control and grazing. Forage crops are plants grown mainly to be cut or grazed as feed, including grasses, legumes and cereals. Pasture is grazed land; forage is the feed.

Grasses include tropical C4 types such as guinea, elephant (Napier), Rhodes and signal grass, and temperate C3 types such as ryegrass and cocksfoot. Legumes include tropical stylo, centro, siratro and lablab, and temperate white clover, red clover and lucerne. Legumes usually give more protein and fix nitrogen; some cause bloat.

sections.heading: Establishment and grazing
sections.text:
Pasture establishment starts with site and species choice, soil testing, land preparation, good seed, sowing depth and season, and weed control. Legume seed is often inoculated with rhizobium. Allow new swards to establish before grazing.

Stocking rate is animals per unit of land; 30 ewes on 15 ha gives 2 ewes per hectare. Carrying capacity is the maximum stocking rate the pasture can support without long-term damage; it varies with rainfall, soil, species and management. Rotational grazing divides the area into paddocks and moves animals, letting each paddock rest and regrow. It improves persistence but needs fencing and planning.

sections.heading: Hay, silage and quality
sections.text:
Hay is cut forage dried to a low moisture so it stores without mould. Silage is cut forage preserved by anaerobic fermentation, usually at higher moisture; acids lower pH and limit spoilage. Both need cutting at the right growth stage, quick wilting or packing, and good storage.

Forage quality is judged by leafiness, stage at harvest, colour and smell, freedom from mould and weeds, and chemical analysis. Young leafy forage is usually more digestible and higher in crude protein. As plants mature, fibre (neutral detergent fibre, NDF, and acid detergent fibre, ADF) rises and digestibility and energy fall. Crude protein is estimated from nitrogen content; NDF indicates fibre bulk and intake; ADF relates to digestibility.

keyPoints: Rangeland and natural pasture are grazed natural vegetation; improved pasture is sown and managed; forage crops are grown for feed.
Tropical grasses are mainly C4 and temperate grasses C3; legumes add protein and fix nitrogen.
Stocking rate = number of animals ÷ area grazed; carrying capacity is the sustainable maximum.
Rotational grazing rests paddocks so plants can regrow.
Hay is dried forage; silage is preserved by anaerobic fermentation.
Judge forage by leafiness, harvest stage and chemical tests such as crude protein, NDF and ADF.

en.title: Farm Animal Anatomy and Physiology
en.short: Body systems of cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and poultry, and how structure guides management.

sections.heading: Systems overview
sections.text: Anatomy is structure; physiology is function. In cattle, sheep, goats and pigs the skeleton supports the body and protects organs. The skeletal system includes bones and joints. The nervous system, including the brain, spinal cord and nerves, coordinates senses and movement. The heart and blood vessels form the circulatory system, and the lungs and airways form the respiratory system. Birds have lightweight bones, a keel for flight muscles, lungs connected to air sacs and no diaphragm. Mammals have a muscular diaphragm. These differences affect restraint: use species-specific methods that support the body and avoid injury.

sections.heading: Digestion
sections.text: Ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats) have a four-compartment stomach: rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum. Microbes in the rumen ferment fibre. They chew the cud and need roughage. Pigs are monogastric, with a simple stomach and less fibre digestion. Poultry have no teeth; feed passes to the crop, proventriculus, gizzard, small intestine, caeca and cloaca. Grit in the gizzard helps grind feed. Feeding must match structure: roughage for ruminants, concentrated diets for pigs and poultry, and suitable particle size for birds.

sections.heading: Reproduction and handling
sections.text: Reproductive organs differ. Mammals have paired ovaries and a bicornuate (two-horned) uterus; pigs are litter-bearing. Poultry have a cloaca, a shared opening for the digestive, urinary and reproductive tracts, and usually only the left ovary and oviduct are functional. Breeding practice uses these facts: heat detection in mammals, and lighting and nesting for poultry. Handling respects senses and flight zones, the distance an animal keeps between itself and a threat. A small case: Amina keeps goats and sheep. Goats browse with mobile lips and narrow muzzles, so she offers cut fodder in racks; sheep graze shorter grass. She moves them calmly, using the flight zone. If she also keeps poultry, she catches them by the body, not the wings.

keyPoints: Anatomy is structure; physiology is function.
Ruminants have four stomach compartments and rely on rumen microbes for fibre.
Pigs are monogastric; poultry use a crop, gizzard and caeca and have no teeth.
Birds have air sacs and no diaphragm; mammals have a muscular diaphragm.
Mammals have a bicornuate uterus; poultry usually have only the left ovary and oviduct functional.
Calm handling uses the flight zone and species-specific restraint to reduce injury.

en.title: Animal Nutrition and Feed Formulation
en.short: Nutrients, proximate analysis, requirements, feedstuffs and simple least-cost ration formulation.

sections.heading: Feed nutrients
sections.text:
Nutrients are what an animal uses from feed. Water carries nutrients and heat. Carbohydrates, mainly starches and sugars, supply energy; ruminants digest fibre with microbes, but pigs and poultry use it poorly.

Fats are concentrated energy and carry fat-soluble vitamins. Proteins supply amino acids for growth, milk, eggs and repair. Minerals build bone and maintain electrolytes; vitamins regulate metabolism. Balance matters, not energy alone.

sections.heading: Proximate analysis
sections.text:
Proximate analysis is the Weende scheme. It reports moisture, crude protein, crude fibre, ether extract (crude fat), ash and nitrogen-free extract (NFE).

Crude protein is nitrogen × 6.25. Ash is mineral residue after burning. NFE is by difference: dry matter − (crude protein + crude fibre + ether extract + ash). The fractions are crude, not pure nutrients, and say little about digestibility. Check whether table values are on a dry matter or as-fed basis.

sections.heading: Requirements and feeds
sections.text:
Maintenance requirement keeps an animal alive with no gain or loss. Production requirement is the extra for growth, milk, eggs, pregnancy or work. Requirements vary with species, weight, age, stage, activity and climate; use current tables for the species and country.

Roughages (pasture, hay, silage) supply fibre. Concentrates (cereals, oilseed meals) supply energy and protein. By-products and mineral or vitamin supplements fill gaps. Additives such as amino acids, enzymes or probiotics are regulated, and approved lists differ by country.

sections.heading: Formulation example
sections.text:
A ration is the daily allowance. The Pearson square balances one nutrient between two feeds. For 100 kg of 16% CP from maize (9% CP) and soybean meal (44% CP): soybean meal parts = 16 − 9 = 7; maize parts = 44 − 16 = 28; total = 35. Soybean meal = 7 ÷ 35 × 100 = 20 kg; maize = 28 ÷ 35 × 100 = 80 kg.

Check: 80 × 0.09 = 7.2 kg CP; 20 × 0.44 = 8.8 kg CP; total = 16.0 kg CP in 100 kg, or 16%. Least cost compares feeds by cost per kg CP (price ÷ CP fraction) and uses linear programming for many feeds and constraints. Values and prices vary; check current tables.

keyPoints: The main nutrients are water, carbohydrates, fats, proteins, minerals and vitamins.
Proximate analysis reports moisture, crude protein, crude fibre, ether extract, ash and nitrogen-free extract.
Crude protein = nitrogen × 6.25; NFE = dry matter − (crude protein + crude fibre + ether extract + ash).
Maintenance keeps the animal alive; production adds growth, milk, eggs, pregnancy or work.
The Pearson square uses opposite differences from the target nutrient level to find feed parts.
Least-cost formulation compares cost per unit of nutrient, for example cost per kg CP = price ÷ CP fraction, and respects all constraints.

en.title: Animal Breeding and Genetics
en.short: Mendelian and quantitative inheritance, heritability, selection, inbreeding and crossbreeding in farm animals.

sections.heading: Inheritance and traits
sections.text: Mendelian inheritance concerns single genes with clear effects, such as coat colour or some defects. An allele is one form of a gene. Each parent passes one allele, so offspring genotypes follow ratios such as 1:2:1 from two heterozygotes. Most production traits, including growth rate, milk yield and litter size, are quantitative: many genes act together, each with small effect, and the environment also matters. Their variation is measured in the population, not by simple ratios. Breeding value is an animal’s value as a parent, estimated from its own records and those of relatives.

sections.heading: Heritability and repeatability
sections.text: Heritability is the share of observed variation due to genetic differences. Narrow-sense heritability, h² = V_A ÷ V_P, uses additive genetic variance V_A, the part passed on reliably; broad-sense H² = V_G ÷ V_P includes all genetic effects. Repeatability is the consistency of repeated records on the same animal. It is the between-animal variance divided by total variance, and it sets an upper limit to heritability. A trait with low heritability responds slowly to selection; a repeatable trait can be culled or selected on fewer records.

sections.heading: Selection and mating
sections.text: Selection methods include mass selection on own performance, family selection, progeny testing for sex-limited traits such as milk yield, and index or BLUP (best linear unbiased prediction) selection, which combines records. Response is R = h²S, where S is the selected parents’ advantage over the population mean. Inbreeding raises homozygosity and can cause inbreeding depression. Hybrid vigour, or heterosis, is the better performance of crossbreds. Mating systems include purebreeding, inbreeding, outcrossing, crossbreeding and grading up.

sections.heading: Upgrading or crossbreeding
sections.text: Upgrading uses a superior purebred sire repeatedly on local dams; it raises productivity while keeping some local adaptation, but needs a steady supply of purebred sires. Crossbreeding uses two or more breeds to gain heterosis and combine strengths, but the crossbred may not suit low-input conditions. Choose by testing under local conditions. Example: if h² = 0.30 and selected parents average 10 kg above the mean, R = 0.30 × 10 = 3 kg. With a 2-year generation interval, annual response is 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 kg per year.

keyPoints: Mendelian traits are controlled by one or few genes; quantitative traits are controlled by many genes and the environment.
Narrow-sense heritability is h² = V_A ÷ V_P; repeatability is between-animal variance ÷ total variance.
Response to selection is R = h²S, where S is the selection differential.
Inbreeding raises homozygosity and can cause inbreeding depression; crossbreeding can produce hybrid vigour.
Upgrading uses repeated purebred sires on local dams; crossbreeding uses two or more breeds and needs testing under local conditions.
Selection can use own performance, family records, progeny testing or BLUP.

en.title: Animal Reproduction and Husbandry
en.short: Oestrous cycles, mating, pregnancy, birth, egg formation and routine care of cattle, sheep, goats and pigs.

sections.heading: Puberty and the cycle
sections.text: Puberty is the age when an animal first shows fertile oestrus (heat); it varies with breed and nutrition. Cattle, sheep, goats and pigs have oestrous cycles, repeated intervals from one heat to the next. Cycles average about 21 days in cattle and pigs, 17 in sheep and 20 in goats, with variation. Poultry have no oestrous cycle. The hen ovulates yolk from the ovary; it passes through the infundibulum, magnum, isthmus and shell gland, where albumen, membranes and shell are added in turn, then the vagina. Egg formation takes about 24 to 26 hours.

sections.heading: Mating and pregnancy
sections.text: Heat detection means watching for standing to be mounted, restlessness, mucus and, in pigs, the standing reflex. Time insemination from detection. Natural mating uses a fertile male. Artificial insemination (AI) places semen in the female tract and needs trained staff, good semen handling and records. Pregnancy diagnosis uses ultrasound in all species, and rectal palpation in cattle where trained. Gestation is about 283 days in cattle, 147 in sheep, 150 in goats and 114 in pigs, with variation. Case: Amina’s cow served on 1 May is due around 8 February.

sections.heading: Birth and newborn
sections.text: Parturition is birth. Signs include restlessness, nesting in pigs, relaxed pelvic ligaments and udder enlargement. Most births need no help; intervene if progress stops. The newborn needs air, warmth, colostrum and a clean navel. Colostrum is first milk, rich in antibodies. Ensure the calf, lamb, kid or piglet suckles soon. Piglets need a warm, dry creep area away from the sow. Record births and check the mother.

sections.heading: Routine husbandry
sections.text: Husbandry includes identification, records, vaccination, parasite control, hoof care, feed and water. Castration removes the testes; dehorning removes horns. Both cause pain, so use the method allowed by local law and welfare codes, with pain relief where required, at the recommended age. Cattle need foot and udder checks; sheep need shearing and foot care; goats need hoof trimming; pigs need health checks.

keyPoints: Puberty is the first fertile heat and varies with breed, nutrition and management.
Cattle, sheep, goats and pigs are polyoestrous (sheep and goats breed seasonally in temperate lands); poultry have no oestrous cycle.
Heat detection and correct timing are essential for natural mating and AI.
Gestation is about 283 days in cattle, 147 in sheep, 150 in goats and 114 in pigs, with normal variation.
Parturition and newborn care focus on progress, warmth, colostrum and cleanliness.
Castration and dehorning are painful; follow local law and welfare codes and use pain relief where required.

en.title: Livestock Health and Disease Control
en.short: How livestock diseases spread, their signs, major African diseases, and prevention by vaccination and biosecurity.

sections.heading: Spread of infection
sections.text: A disease agent leaves an infected animal and enters a susceptible one. Routes include direct contact, droplets, contaminated feed or water, and vectors such as ticks, tsetse flies and mosquitoes. Fomites (boots, vehicles), carrier animals that look healthy, wildlife and animal movement also spread infection. Overcrowding and poor ventilation raise risk. Zoonotic diseases, such as brucellosis and anthrax, pass from animals to people. Report suspected notifiable diseases.

sections.heading: Recognising illness
sections.text: Watch the group and individuals. Early signs include dullness, reduced feed or water intake, fever, coughing, nasal discharge, diarrhoea, lameness, skin lumps, abortion and falling milk or egg yield. Several cases or sudden deaths suggest an outbreak. Case: a farmer in Ogun State, Nigeria finds 20 of 500 birds dull, with greenish diarrhoea. Isolate them, clean and disinfect, and call a veterinarian. Do not guess at medicine or dose.

sections.heading: Major disease groups
sections.text: Bacterial diseases include anthrax, blackleg, brucellosis and mastitis. Viral diseases include foot-and-mouth disease, lumpy skin disease, peste des petits ruminants, African swine fever and Newcastle disease. Parasitic diseases are common. Tick-borne diseases include East Coast fever, anaplasmosis, babesiosis and heartwater. Trypanosomiasis is caused by trypanosomes spread by tsetse flies and causes anaemia and wasting. Helminthosis means worm infestation, including roundworms, liver flukes and tapeworms; it causes poor growth and anaemia. Nutritional diseases come from shortages or imbalances, such as mineral deficiency, and are not infectious.

sections.heading: Prevention and biosecurity
sections.text: Vaccination protects only against diseases in the vaccine, and only if the cold chain and dose are correct. Schedules vary by country, vaccine and manufacturer, so follow the national veterinary authority and the label; do not copy another farm’s schedule. Examples include Newcastle disease and infectious bursal disease vaccines, given early with boosters. Biosecurity means keeping agents out: quarantine new animals, limit visitors, disinfect boots and vehicles, control ticks and tsetse, keep feed and water clean, and isolate sick animals. Deworm correctly; observe withdrawal periods.

keyPoints: Disease spreads by direct contact, contaminated feed or water, vectors, fomites, carriers and animal movement.
Early signs include dullness, reduced feed or water intake, fever, diarrhoea, coughing, lameness and falling production.
Tick-borne diseases, trypanosomiasis and helminthosis are major parasitic problems in African livestock.
Vaccination protects only against included diseases and depends on correct cold chain and dose.
Vaccination schedules and notifiable disease rules vary by country; follow the national veterinary authority.
Biosecurity, vector control, quarantine, isolation and responsible drug use reduce disease spread.

en.title: Poultry Production
en.short: Housing systems, bird classes, brooding, lighting, feeding, egg handling, records and small-unit economics.

sections.heading: Housing systems
sections.text:
Free range keeps birds outdoors with shelter. It suits local breeds and is cheap, but feed conversion is poorer and predators, parasites and egg loss are harder to control. Deep litter houses birds on a floor of dry litter such as wood shavings. It is common in small units and allows scratching, but wet litter releases ammonia and invites disease.

Battery cages are small wire cages, often stacked. They save space and simplify egg collection, but they restrict movement and are banned or being phased out in some countries, so check local rules.

sections.heading: Classes of birds
sections.text:
Broilers are meat birds, usually killed at about five to seven weeks in commercial systems. Layers are kept for eggs and begin laying around 18 to 22 weeks, depending on breed and management. Dual purpose birds give both meat and eggs, less of each than specialised types.

Local breeds are hardy and suit free range and low inputs, but grow slowly and lay fewer eggs. A pullet is a young female before laying; a cockerel is a young male.

sections.heading: Brooding and lighting
sections.text:
Brooding is the care of chicks in their first weeks, when they cannot control body temperature. They need warmth, clean water, starter feed and protection. Chicks huddled under the heat source are cold; chicks spread to the edges are too hot. Reduce heat gradually as feathers grow.

Lighting controls day length: long days stimulate laying, short days slow it. Broilers often get near-continuous light to encourage feeding. Exact hours vary, so follow the breed guide.

sections.heading: Feeding, eggs and records
sections.text:
Feeding follows phases: chick starter, grower, then layer or finisher feed. Feed is the largest cost. Collect eggs often, clean them dry, store them cool and sell them fresh. Keep daily records of feed, deaths, eggs and sales.

Feed conversion ratio (FCR) = feed eaten ÷ output. Example: 200 broilers eat 800 kg feed and reach 400 kg live weight. FCR = 800 ÷ 400 = 2.0. If feed costs 500 per kg, feed costs 400,000; at 1,200 per kg live weight, sales are 480,000, leaving 80,000 before other costs. Use your own local prices.

keyPoints: Free range, deep litter and battery cages differ in cost, welfare and disease control.
Broilers are for meat; layers are for eggs; dual purpose birds give both.
Local breeds are hardy but slower growing and lower laying.
Brooding supplies heat until chicks can control their own temperature.
Long day length stimulates egg laying; lighting programmes vary by breed.
Feed conversion ratio = feed eaten ÷ output; feed is usually the largest cost.

en.title: Fisheries and Aquaculture
en.short: Capture fisheries versus fish farming, pond, tank, cage and pen systems, stocking, feeding, water quality and disease.

sections.heading: Capture and culture
sections.text: Capture fisheries harvest wild fish from rivers, lakes and seas. The catch depends on natural production and is limited by quotas, seasons and gear rules. Aquaculture, or fish farming, raises fish under controlled conditions. It can be intensive and reliable, but needs capital, feed, water and disease control. The two are linked: hatcheries may supply fingerlings, and farms may release or escape fish.

sections.heading: Systems and sites
sections.text: Four common systems are the earthen pond, concrete tank, cage and pen. An earthen pond is a dug, embanked pond, usually fertilised to grow plankton. A concrete tank is small, durable and easy to drain. A cage floats in a lake or river and holds fish in netting; a pen encloses part of a water body with a barrier. Site selection considers water quantity and quality, soil that holds water, gentle slope for drainage, flood risk, access and security. Construction provides an inlet, outlet and safe depth. Fertilisation with manure or compost encourages natural food, but must not pollute the water.

sections.heading: Stocking, feed, water
sections.text: Choose species that suit the climate and market, such as tilapia, catfish or carp, and prefer local species where possible. Stocking rate depends on species, size, system and aeration; follow local extension advice. Example: a pond 20 m × 15 m = 300 m². At 3 fish per m², stock 900 fingerlings. If average weight is 50 g, biomass is 900 × 50 g = 45 kg. At 3% body weight per day, feed 45 kg × 0.03 = 1.35 kg daily. Feed quality and amount affect growth and waste. Check dissolved oxygen, pH, temperature and ammonia; low oxygen kills fish quickly.

sections.heading: Harvest and disease
sections.text: Harvest by draining, seining or trapping, and handle fish gently. Common problems include bacterial infections, fungal growth and parasites. Prevent them with clean water, suitable stocking, quarantine of new fish and removal of dead fish. Unusual deaths or lesions should be checked by a fish health specialist.

keyPoints: Capture fisheries harvest wild stocks; aquaculture raises fish under controlled conditions.
Earthen ponds, concrete tanks, cages and pens differ in cost, water use and control.
Site selection needs reliable water, water-holding soil, drainage, access and security.
Stocking number = pond area × stocking rate; feed per day = total biomass × feeding rate.
Water quality, especially dissolved oxygen, pH and ammonia, limits fish survival and growth.
Prevent disease with clean water, sensible stocking, quarantine and prompt removal of dead fish.

en.title: Forestry, Agroforestry and Wildlife Management
en.short: Forest types, sustainable management, tropical agroforestry and wildlife conservation basics.

sections.heading: Forest types and functions
sections.text:
A forest is a community of trees, plants, animals and soil organisms. Forest types follow climate and soil: tropical rainforest, savanna woodland, mangrove, montane forest and plantations. Natural forests self-regenerate; plantations are planted.

Forests have ecological functions such as carbon storage, water cycling, soil protection and habitat. They have economic functions such as timber, fuelwood, poles, food and medicine, and social functions such as recreation and employment.

sections.heading: Sustainable management
sections.text:
