Sustainable forest management means using forests to keep productivity and biodiversity. The key idea is sustained yield: harvest no more than the forest grows. Regeneration may be natural, from seed fall, coppice or root suckers, or artificial, by planting. Protection covers fire breaks and early fire control, pest and grazing control, and enforcement against illegal logging. A management plan sets the rotation, allowable cut and regeneration method.

For example, a 4 ha woodlot grows 8 m³ per ha per year. Annual growth is 4 × 8 = 32 m³. An allowable cut below 32 m³ leaves a safety margin.

sections.heading: Tropical agroforestry
sections.text:
Agroforestry is growing trees with crops or livestock on the same land. Trees can give shade, mulch, fodder, fruit and fuelwood, and may improve soil. Alley cropping uses rows of trees or shrubs with crops between them; prunings become mulch or fodder. Boundary planting puts trees along field edges, giving products while taking little crop space. Homegardens and parkland are other tropical systems.

Species and spacing must suit rainfall, soil and local needs, because trees can compete with crops for water and light.

sections.heading: Wildlife conservation
sections.text:
Wildlife conservation aims to keep species and habitats viable. On farmland, practices include keeping hedges, trees, ponds and field margins, reducing pesticide harm, and leaving corridors that connect habitats. A game reserve is a protected area where wild animals are conserved and may be used for regulated hunting or tourism; rules differ by country.

Community-based management shares benefits with local people and can reduce conflict. Monitoring and buffer zones help.

keyPoints: Forest types depend on climate and soil, and forests have ecological, economic and social functions.
Sustainable forest management keeps productivity and biodiversity by harvesting no more than growth.
Annual growth = area × growth per hectare; the allowable cut should stay below this.
Regeneration is natural (seed, coppice, root suckers) or artificial (planting).
Agroforestry combines trees with crops or livestock; alley cropping and boundary planting are tropical examples.
Wildlife conservation needs habitat, corridors, protected areas and community involvement; game reserve rules differ by country.

en.title: Agricultural Economics and Farm Management
en.short: Farm records, costs, gross margin, partial and enterprise budgets, and linear programming for enterprise mix.

sections.heading: Records, costs and profit
sections.text: Farm records are written facts: areas, inputs, yields, livestock, labour and sales. Physical records give quantities; financial records give values. Accounts include the income statement (revenue and expenses over a period), the balance sheet (assets, liabilities and equity at a date) and cash flow (money in and out). Variable costs change with output, such as seed, fertiliser, feed and casual labour. Fixed costs do not change with output in the short run, such as land rent, machinery depreciation and permanent staff. Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost. Revenue = price × quantity sold. Profit = total revenue − total cost. Depreciation allocates an asset’s cost over its life; it is not a cash payment.

sections.heading: Gross margin and partial budgets
sections.text: Gross margin = gross output − variable costs for one enterprise. It is the return to fixed costs and profit. Example: 2,000 kg maize at 250 currency units per kg gives 500,000. Variable costs are seed 40,000, fertiliser 90,000, labour 70,000 and other 20,000, total 220,000. Gross margin = 500,000 − 220,000 = 280,000. A partial budget tests one change: add extra returns and reduced costs, subtract extra costs and reduced returns. A positive balance favours the change, subject to risk and cash flow.

sections.heading: Enterprise mix and linear programming
sections.text: Enterprise budgets compare whole enterprises. Farm size and labour use interact: large farms may mechanise to save labour; small farms rely on family labour. Labour peaks at planting and harvest, so the labour calendar constrains the plan. Linear programming chooses enterprise areas to maximise total gross margin subject to land, labour, capital and rotation limits. It assumes fixed coefficients, linearity, divisibility and certainty. Example: maximise 280,000M + 180,000B subject to M + B <= 10 and 60M + 40B <= 480, where M and B are hectares of maize and beans. The best corner is M = 8, B = 0, margin 2,240,000; M = 4, B = 6 gives 2,200,000.

keyPoints: Gross margin = gross output − variable costs; it is the return to fixed costs.
Profit = total revenue − total cost, and total cost = fixed cost + variable cost.
Revenue = price × quantity sold.
A partial budget compares added returns and reduced costs with added costs and reduced returns.
Enterprise budgets compare whole enterprises; linear programming chooses an enterprise mix subject to constraints.
Linear programming assumes fixed input-output coefficients, linearity, divisibility and certainty.

en.title: Agricultural Marketing and Cooperatives
en.short: Marketing functions, middlemen and boards, price margins, and farmers’ cooperatives.

sections.heading: Marketing functions
sections.text: Agricultural marketing covers all activities from the farm gate to the consumer. Assembly means collecting small lots from many farms into larger, saleable quantities. Storage holds produce across time; it costs money and risks loss. Transport moves produce to markets. Processing changes form, such as drying or milling. Grading sorts produce by quality so buyers can trust it. Selling finds buyers, sets terms and transfers ownership. Each function adds value but also adds cost.

sections.heading: Middlemen, boards and prices
sections.text:
Middlemen include assemblers, wholesalers, retailers and brokers. They perform marketing functions and earn a margin. A commodity board is a statutory body that regulates, buys or promotes a named crop; its role varies by country and many boards have been reformed or closed. Prices depend on supply, demand, quality, season, location, information and bargaining power. Market margin = retail price − farm-gate price. Farmer’s share = farm-gate price ÷ retail price × 100.

Example: 100 kg sells at 200 per kg farm-gate, giving 20,000; retail at 350 per kg gives 35,000. Margin = 15,000. Margin as % of retail = 15,000 ÷ 35,000 × 100 = 42.9%. Farmer’s share = 20,000 ÷ 35,000 × 100 = 57.1%. Seasonal prices often fall at harvest and rise in the lean season because of storage costs, losses and demand.

sections.heading: Farmers’ cooperatives
sections.text: A cooperative is a member-owned business run democratically for mutual benefit. Formation starts with a common need, then registration under national cooperative law, written bylaws, and election of a board. Management rests with the general meeting, board and paid manager. Accounts must be audited and reported. Financing comes from member shares, savings, retained surplus, bank loans and sometimes grants. Cooperatives can bulk-buy inputs and market produce together, raising bargaining power.

keyPoints: Marketing functions are assembly, storage, transport, processing, grading and selling; each adds value and cost.
Middlemen earn a margin for performing these functions, not simply for adding a mark-up.
Market margin = retail price − farm-gate price; farmer’s share = farm-gate price ÷ retail price × 100.
Seasonal prices often fall at harvest and rise in the lean season because of storage costs, losses and demand.
Commodity boards are statutory bodies whose roles vary by country; check the current body and rules.
A farmers’ cooperative is member-owned and democratically controlled; it needs clear bylaws, audited accounts and mixed financing from shares, surplus and loans.

en.title: Agricultural Extension and Rural Sociology
en.short: How extension teaches farmers, how rural society shapes adoption, and how technology reaches farms.

sections.heading: What extension means
sections.text: Agricultural extension is informal education for rural people. The agent does not farm for the farmer; the agent brings information, teaches skills and helps people decide for themselves. Rural sociology is the study of rural social structure: the families, age groups, religious bodies, cooperatives and leadership patterns that shape how a village decides. Extension works through these structures.

sections.heading: Extension methods
sections.text: Demonstration shows a practice on a plot. A method demonstration teaches a skill step by step. A result demonstration compares new and old practice side by side, so farmers see the difference. Farm visits let the agent meet the farmer’s real conditions. Field days bring a group to a demonstration site for seeing, questions and discussion. Training and visits (T and V) is a system where agents get in-service training and visit a fixed list of contact farmers on a timetable. Radio and mobile phones reach many people cheaply, but they stay one-way unless a feedback channel exists.

sections.heading: Groups and adoption
sections.text: Farmers learn from people they trust. Farmer groups such as cooperatives, thrift societies and village associations lower the cost of reaching many farmers and give members credit, buying power and a voice. Adoption is the decision to use an innovation regularly. Rogers described five adopter groups, from innovators to laggards, giving an S-shaped adoption curve over time. Adoption is faster when the innovation has clear relative advantage, fits existing practice, is simple, can be tried on a small plot, and gives visible results.

sections.heading: Case and technology transfer
sections.text: An agent in a village of 40 farmers demonstrates an improved maize variety. After one season 24 farmers plant it: 24 ÷ 40 × 100 = 60 per cent. After the second season 34 do: 34 ÷ 40 × 100 = 85 per cent. Research institutes breed and test such varieties; extension carries them to farms, and farmers’ problems travel back. This two-way link is technology transfer. In Nigeria, public extension runs mainly through the state Agricultural Development Programmes (ADPs).

keyPoints: Extension is informal education that helps farmers decide and act for themselves.
A method demonstration teaches a skill; a result demonstration compares new and old practice.
Training and visits gives agents regular training and a fixed visiting timetable.
Adoption follows an S-shaped curve, from innovators through to laggards.
Innovations spread faster when they show relative advantage, are simple, can be tried and give visible results.
Extension is a two-way link: research institutes supply technology, farmers supply problems.

en.title: Post-Harvest Handling, Storage and Processing
en.short: Causes of post-harvest losses, drying, storage, pest control and simple processing.

sections.heading: Losses and causes
sections.text: Post-harvest loss is the reduction in quantity or quality after harvest. Causes are biological, mechanical and environmental. Grains lose through high moisture, moulds, insects, rodents, cracking in threshing and delayed drying. Roots and tubers bruise, sprout, lose water and rot; curing heals skin wounds. Fruits and vegetables respire, transpire, produce ethylene, a ripening gas, and suffer chilling injury, crushing and decay. Animal products such as milk, meat, fish and eggs spoil through bacteria, enzymes, oxidation and poor temperature control. Losses are worst when handling and storage are rushed.

sections.heading: Drying and storage
sections.text: Drying lowers moisture so microbes and insects cannot grow. Safe moisture differs by crop and climate; follow advice. Threshing separates grain from cobs, pods or panicles; winnowing uses air to remove chaff. Clean, dry grain stores better. Traditional stores include mud granaries, cribs and sacks; they are cheap but let in moisture and pests. Hermetic storage uses sealed airtight containers or bags. Insects use up oxygen and die, and mould slows. Store pest control starts with cleaning, drying, inspection and rodent-proofing. Use approved insecticides or fumigants only as directed, by trained people.

sections.heading: Simple processing
sections.text: Milling grinds grain into flour or meal; removing bran and germ keeps better but loses nutrients. Oil extraction presses oil from seeds, nuts or fruit; mechanical pressing is simple, solvent extraction industrial. Fermentation uses bacteria, yeasts or moulds to change food. It can improve keeping quality and flavour, as in cassava, milk and cereals, but must be controlled. Pasteurisation heats a liquid, usually milk, to kill pathogens and most spoilage organisms, then cools it quickly. It does not sterilise, so the product still needs refrigeration.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A farmer harvests 1,000 kg of maize. Drying and handling lose 50 kg, and storage insects and mould lose 30 kg. Total loss = 50 + 30 = 80 kg. Percentage loss = (80 ÷ 1,000) × 100 = 8%. 920 kg remain. If hermetic storage prevented 30 kg loss, loss would be 5%.

keyPoints: Post-harvest losses arise from biological, mechanical and environmental causes, and are worst with delay, moisture and damage.
Drying to safe moisture, threshing and winnowing prepare grain for storage; safe moisture varies by crop and climate.
Traditional stores are cheap but permeable; hermetic storage is sealed and controls insects by oxygen depletion.
Store pest control relies on cleaning, drying, inspection, rodent-proofing and correct use of approved chemicals.
Milling, oil extraction, fermentation and pasteurisation change or preserve food, but pasteurisation does not sterilise.
Percentage loss = (lost quantity ÷ harvested quantity) × 100; in the example, 80 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 8%.

en.title: Agricultural Ethics, Safety and Regulation
en.short: Professional conduct, pesticide and machinery safety, food standards, environmental duties and regulators.

sections.heading: Professional conduct
sections.text: Agricultural ethics is the set of standards for honest and responsible practice. Keep records that are true and complete: spray dates, products and rates, animal treatments, harvests and sales. False records mislead buyers, regulators and your own management. Respect farm workers by giving clear training, safe equipment, fair treatment and the right to refuse unsafe work. Responsibility to consumers means producing food that is safe, correctly labelled and traceable, meaning it can be followed back to the farm.

sections.heading: Pesticides and machinery
sections.text: Read the label before using any pesticide, a chemical used to kill pests. Wear the personal protective equipment (PPE) the label requires, calibrate the sprayer, avoid spraying in strong wind, and observe the withholding period, the time between the last spray and harvest. Store products locked away and never reuse containers. For machinery, keep guards and power take-off shields in place, switch off before clearing blockages, and train operators. Example: a label says 2 L per hectare in 200 L water. For 0.5 ha: 2 × 0.5 = 1 L product in 200 × 0.5 = 100 L water.

sections.heading: Food safety and environment
sections.text: Food safety and quality standards cover hygiene, grading, labelling, moisture and contaminant limits. Many countries base their rules on Codex Alimentarius, the international food standards set by the UN food and health agencies. Traceability and good agricultural practice (GAP) help. Environmental duties include protecting water, soil, bees and neighbours from drift, and disposing of containers correctly. Do not let short-term yield pressure justify lasting damage.

sections.heading: Regulation and checking
sections.text: Agrochemicals are normally registered, meaning a national authority approves each product and its label for stated uses. Produce may need certification, such as a phytosanitary certificate, which confirms plant health for trade and is issued by the national plant protection organisation. For example, Nigeria’s NAFDAC regulates food, drugs and chemicals, and the United States Environmental Protection Agency registers pesticides. Rules, names and limits differ by country and change, so check your own country’s current official sources before you act.

keyPoints: Keep spray, treatment and harvest records honest and complete.
Respect workers through training, protective equipment and the right to refuse unsafe work.
Read the pesticide label, wear the required PPE and follow the withholding period.
Guards and shields on machinery stay in place, and machines are switched off before clearing.
Food safety and quality rules often follow Codex Alimentarius, but national limits differ.
Check your country’s current agrochemical registration and produce certification rules before acting.

en.title: Research Methods and the Final Project
en.short: Framing a problem and hypothesis, reviewing literature, designing experiments, sampling, statistics and writing up.

sections.heading: Problem and literature
sections.text:
A research problem is the gap between what is known and what your study must find out. State it as one clear question that a small project can answer. A hypothesis is a testable prediction, often a null hypothesis that treatments do not differ. Name the variables, population and setting in your objectives.

Review literature to learn methods, avoid repeating work and show the gap. Use primary papers and official reports, and record every source.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text:
An experiment compares treatments while controlling other factors. In the field, use uniform plots, guard rows and equal management apart from the treatment. In the laboratory, control temperature, light and contamination. Sampling means taking a small part to represent the whole; define the sampling unit and population. Randomisation means assigning treatments or samples by chance, so bias is not built in. Replication means repeating each treatment on independent units; it estimates error.

Use a completely randomised design in uniform conditions, or a randomised complete block design when soil or shade varies. Record data on dated sheets, with units and codes, and back up files. For three plots yielding 2.0, 2.4 and 2.8 t/ha: mean = 7.2 ÷ 3 = 2.4 t/ha; squared deviations sum to 0.32; sample variance = 0.32 ÷ 2 = 0.16; standard deviation (spread) = √0.16 = 0.4 t/ha; standard error (uncertainty of the mean) = 0.4 ÷ √3 = 0.23 t/ha.

sections.heading: Analysis and writing
sections.text:
Describe data with the mean, range and standard deviation. A t-test compares two means; analysis of variance (ANOVA) compares several. Report the test and sample size, and do not treat a small difference as proof of no effect.

The final project has a title, abstract, introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Write methods so another student could repeat the work. Present tables and figures with clear labels and units. In a seminar, state the problem, design, main result and limitation. Check your institution’s format and submission rules.

keyPoints: A research problem is a clear question; a hypothesis is a testable prediction, often a null hypothesis of no difference.
A literature review should use primary sources and show the gap your study fills.
Randomisation helps prevent bias in treatment assignment; replication gives an estimate of experimental error.
Sampling must define the unit and population; record data with units, dates and codes.
Mean = sum of values ÷ n; sample variance = sum of squared deviations ÷ (n − 1); standard error = standard deviation ÷ √n.
Report the test and sample size, and write methods so the work could be repeated.

en.title: Advanced Crop Physiology and Stress Biology
en.short: Membrane, hormone and gene responses to drought, heat, salinity, flooding and nutrient stress.

sections.heading: Sensing and signals
sections.text:
Stress begins when conditions exceed a crop’s tolerance. Drought and salinity lower water potential, heat changes membrane fluidity, flooding removes oxygen, and nutrient shortage limits growth. Plants sense these through membranes, calcium signals and reactive oxygen species (ROS).

Hormones coordinate responses. Abscisic acid (ABA) closes stomata and activates drought genes. Ethylene accumulates in flooded roots and helps form aerenchyma, gas spaces that carry oxygen. Transcription factors such as DREB/CBF change gene expression, switching on stress-responsive genes.

sections.heading: Membranes and osmotic adjustment
sections.text:
Heat and drought make membranes leaky; heat shock proteins help. Salinity has two phases: osmotic stress, then ion toxicity. Plants may exclude sodium at the root or store it in vacuoles.

To keep water entering, cells adjust osmotically by accumulating compatible solutes such as proline, glycine betaine and sugars. Osmotic adjustment lowers cell water potential without harming metabolism. In flooding, oxygen shortage shifts metabolism to fermentation, and ethylene and auxin changes allow aerenchyma to form. Nutrient stress alters roots and transporters.

sections.heading: Antioxidants and water use
sections.text:
Stress produces ROS that damage lipids, proteins and DNA. Antioxidants include enzymes such as superoxide dismutase, catalase and peroxidase, plus ascorbate and glutathione.

Water use efficiency (WUE) is yield or biomass divided by water used. Example: 4,000 kg/ha yield with 500 mm water uses 500 × 10 = 5,000 m³/ha. WUE = 4,000 ÷ 5,000 = 0.8 kg/m³. High WUE can come from lower stomatal conductance, deeper roots or a higher harvest index, but not always with high yield.

sections.heading: Breeding and management
sections.text:
Breeding uses stress nurseries, controlled environments and marker-assisted selection.

Traits include stay-green, root depth, osmotic adjustment, sodium exclusion and heat tolerance. Gene expression studies suggest candidate genes, but field testing is essential because stress varies. Management matches crop to environment: early planting to escape heat, mulching and deficit irrigation for drought, raised beds and drainage for flooding, leaching for salinity, gypsum for sodic soils where sodium is held on soil particles, and site-specific fertiliser.

keyPoints: Stress responses begin with sensing at membranes, calcium and ROS signals, then hormone and gene-expression changes.
ABA drives stomatal closure and drought gene expression; ethylene helps flooded roots form aerenchyma.
Osmotic adjustment uses compatible solutes to lower cell water potential and maintain turgor.
Antioxidant enzymes and ascorbate or glutathione protect cells from ROS damage.
WUE = yield or biomass ÷ water used; for example 4,000 kg/ha ÷ 5,000 m³/ha = 0.8 kg/m³.
Breeding and management must be tested in the field because stress varies.

en.title: Advanced Plant and Animal Breeding
en.short: Covers quantitative genetics, GxE, indices, breeding values, mating designs, polyploidy, hybrids and genomic tools.

sections.heading: Breeding value and GxE
sections.text: A breeding value (BV) is the additive genetic merit passed to offspring; with random mates it is estimated as twice the deviation of progeny mean from the population mean. Heritability (h²) is the share of phenotypic variance that is additive genetic. Response to selection is R = h²S, where S is the selection differential, or R = i h σA. Genotype by environment interaction (GxE) means genotypes rank differently across environments, so selection in one environment may not transfer to another.

sections.heading: Indices and mating
sections.text: A selection index combines measured traits into one score, I = b1P1 + b2P2 + …, with weights chosen to maximise correlation with an aggregate objective H = a1G1 + a2G2 + …. Mating designs structure crosses: diallel, factorial, topcross and testcross. Progeny testing evaluates a parent by its offspring, as with dairy bulls. BLUP (best linear unbiased prediction) uses family and performance records to estimate BVs.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A dairy herd averages 500 kg of milk per lactation. A bull mated to random cows sires 20 daughters that average 540 kg. Assuming equal environments and no selection, his estimated BV is 2 × (540 − 500) = 80 kg. If h² = 0.30 and parents are selected 2.0 kg above the mean, R = 0.30 × 2.0 = 0.60 kg. The progeny mean should rise by 0.60 kg, not 2.0 kg, because only the additive part is inherited.

sections.heading: Hybrids and genomic tools
sections.text: Polyploids carry more than two chromosome sets; allele dosage and segregation are complex, so breeding values need dosage-aware models. Hybrid breeding exploits heterosis (hybrid vigour), often using male sterility. Marker-assisted selection (MAS) uses DNA markers linked to major genes and works best for simple traits. Genomic selection (GS) predicts BVs from many markers, using a reference population with genotypes and phenotypes. In low-input settings GS is limited by small reference populations, high costs, strong GxE and poor local validation; MAS misses small-effect traits.

keyPoints: Breeding value is additive genetic merit; with random mates, BV = 2 × (progeny mean − population mean).
Response to selection is R = h²S, or R = i h σA, where S is the selection differential.
GxE means genotype rankings change across environments, so broad adaptation must be tested.
A selection index scores I = b1P1 + b2P2 + … to predict an aggregate objective H = a1G1 + a2G2 + ….
Mating designs such as diallel, factorial, topcross and testcross, plus progeny testing, reveal combining ability and parent merit.
MAS suits major genes; genomic selection needs a good reference population and is limited in low-input systems by cost, small reference sets, GxE and weak validation.

en.title: Sustainable Agriculture and Natural Resource Management
en.short: Sustainable intensification, ISFM, IPM, climate-smart farming, nutrient budgets and land restoration.

sections.heading: Four connected principles
sections.text: Sustainable intensification means raising output per hectare on land already farmed, while cutting harm per unit of output, instead of clearing new land. Integrated soil fertility management (ISFM) combines mineral fertiliser with organic matter and improved seed, adapted to the local soil and climate; the aim is fertiliser use efficiency, not maximum fertiliser. Integrated pest management (IPM) combines resistant varieties, rotation, biological control and scouting, using pesticides only above an economic threshold. Climate-smart agriculture (CSA) pursues three goals together: productivity, adaptation and mitigation.

sections.heading: Cycles and on-farm biodiversity
sections.text: Carbon and nutrient cycling: residues, manure and roots build soil organic matter, which holds water and cations, and decomposers release nitrogen and phosphorus slowly. Nutrients leave through leaching, erosion, volatilisation and denitrification. Farm biodiversity includes pollinators, natural enemies of pests, soil organisms and trees; hedgerows and agroforestry support these and add litter and shade.

sections.heading: Land degradation and restoration
sections.text: Land degradation is loss of soil productivity through erosion, nutrient mining, salinisation, compaction or falling organic matter. Restoration uses organic inputs, cover crops, terracing, reduced tillage and agroforestry, plus liming or drainage where needed. Recovery is slow, so prevention is cheaper than cure.

sections.heading: Trade-offs and a worked budget
sections.text:
Trade-offs are real: higher yield may mean more fertiliser and emissions; an organic premium may not cover a lower yield; short-term profit can mine soil capital. A nutrient budget makes this visible.

Continuous maize at 2 t/ha, no inputs. Grain holds about 15 kg N per tonne, so 2 × 15 = 30 kg N/ha exported. Add 10 kg N/ha lost to leaching and erosion. Natural inputs give about 5 kg N/ha.

Balance = 5 − (30 + 10) = −35 kg N/ha per year.

With ISFM: 50 kg fertiliser N + 25 kg N from a cowpea rotation + 10 kg manure + 5 kg natural inputs = 90 kg in. A 3 t/ha crop exports 45 kg and 35 kg are lost, so 80 kg out. Balance = +10 kg N/ha.

keyPoints: Sustainable intensification raises yield per hectare while reducing harm per unit of output.
ISFM pairs mineral fertiliser with organic matter and good seed to raise nutrient use efficiency.
IPM puts pesticides last, after scouting and non-chemical controls.
CSA must deliver productivity, adaptation and mitigation together.
A nutrient budget compares inputs with removals and losses to show whether soil is being mined.
Restoring degraded land is slow and costly, so prevention is preferred.

en.title: Advanced Agricultural Research Methods and Dissertation
en.short: Design, modelling, on-farm trials, ethics, writing and planning a master’s dissertation.

sections.heading: Designs for trials
sections.text: A factorial experiment tests all combinations of levels of two or more factors. It estimates main effects and interactions. A 2 × 3 factorial has 6 combinations; with 4 replicates it needs 24 plots. The interaction degrees of freedom are (2−1)(3−1)=2. A split plot suits factors that are hard to change, such as tillage, and factors that are easy to change, such as variety. The hard factor goes on main plots and the easy factor on subplots, giving two error terms. With 2 main treatments, 3 sub treatments and 4 blocks, main-plot error df = (4−1)(2−1)=3 and subplot error df = 2(4−1)(3−1)=12. Repeated measures design records the same plot or animal over time; observations are correlated, so do not treat time as independent.

sections.heading: Models and variables
sections.text: Mixed models contain fixed effects, such as treatment means, and random effects, such as blocks, plots or animals, which are assumed drawn from a population. They give correct standard errors for split-plot and repeated-measures data. Multivariate methods analyse several correlated responses together. Principal component analysis reduces many variables to a few composite axes; MANOVA tests treatment effects on a set of responses. Use them when separate univariate tests would mislead.

sections.heading: On-farm and ethics
sections.text: On-farm trials test technologies in farmers’ fields, where soil and management vary. Randomise within sites and use several sites. Participatory methods involve farmers in choosing treatments, scoring plots and interpreting results. Research ethics requires informed consent, privacy, fair benefit and honest reporting. Obtain permits before collecting data, moving biological material or working with animals; rules differ by country, so check the current national authority.

sections.heading: Writing and dissertation
sections.text: Scientific writing uses clear structure: introduction, methods, results and discussion. Report design, randomisation, model and software so others can repeat the work. Plan the dissertation early: refine the question, write a protocol, agree supervision, set a timeline, manage data and leave time for analysis and revision. Execute in stages and keep records.

keyPoints: Factorial designs test all combinations and estimate interactions; interaction df = (a−1)(b−1).
Split plots use two error terms; main-plot error df = (r−1)(a−1) and subplot error df = a(r−1)(b−1).
Repeated measures need models that account for correlation within the same unit over time.
Mixed models separate fixed treatment effects from random block, plot or animal effects.
Multivariate methods such as PCA and MANOVA handle several correlated responses together.
On-farm trials need randomisation, several sites, farmer participation, ethics approval and permits.
